searchText: We won't ever delete the special case hashing on type 0 transactions (where the hash trims off the wrapper byte). All the blocks between Berlin and London will have to be re-validated. A special hashing rule will live forever. Unless we can regenisis. Also, a client could decide to just hard code the details of block `n` and not sync history before it, thus not need to actually implement all of the old behavior. One can also imagine a client I implementation where each hard fork coincided with a full client fork (of the source code fork variety) where they essentially have a different codebase for each network hard fork, and they all share a DB and have a mechanism of switching clients on network fork blocks. Such a client would be able to have clean code for their newer stuff as the latest version wouldn't need to understand legacy blocks. Point here being merely that I think technical debt for code that was used in old blocks has a different cost than code necessary to process/handle new blocks/transactions. > Also, a client could decide to just hard code the details of block n and not sync history before it, thus not need to actually implement all of the old behavior. But they won't. Weak subjectivity isn't good enough for some people. > Also, a client could decide to just hard code the details of block n and not sync history before it, thus not need to actually implement all of the old behavior. I thought about this a while back, but with a caveat: to have an "coredev approved EIP" stating the new hash of some recent block, like block 10 million. There were two outcomes of that discussion: 1. lets just wait for regenesis to handle this programatically; 2. have something like the flyclient sync in place.
